query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the ability of the reactive element X to form a slow-growing, adherent oxide in synergy with Cr. When X is Al or Si, the formation of thermodynamically stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2, along with Cr2O3) limits the outward flux of metal cations and minimizes internal stresses, thereby yielding a protective, crack‐free scale. In contrast, when X is Mn, the tendency to form less protective, more volatile Mn oxides leads to rapid scale growth, higher stress accumulation, and consequently scale cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: Prolonged isothermal oxidation at >900 °C under oxygen-rich conditions
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, slow-growing oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3/SiO2 in combination with Cr2O3) that acts as a barrier to further diffusion
generation.mechanism: When X is Al or Si, stable oxide formation reduces cation and oxygen diffusion rates, limiting internal stress development and microcrack formation at the alloy/oxide interface. Conversely, when X is Mn, formation of less adherent and volatile oxides fails to control elemental diffusion and stress accumulation, leading to scale spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will develop a thin, adherent, and slow-growing protective oxide layer with minimal cracking, while alloys with X = Mn will exhibit faster oxide growth, increased microcracking, and spallation of the protective scale.
generation.baseline: Comparison against a CrFeCoNi alloy lacking the reactive element X or containing Mn, which is expected to form unstable oxide layers
generation.boundary: Valid for high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase solid-solution states subjected to oxidation above 900 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive environments over extended durations
generation.uncertainty: Precise diffusion coefficients, stress evolution kinetics, and the quantitative impact of phase interactions on oxide adherence require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X systematically varied among Al, Si, and Mn. Subject these samples to prolonged isothermal oxidation tests at temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxygen-rich atmosphere. Characterize the oxide scale morphology, composition, and adherence using techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Compare the oxide growth kinetics, crack density, and incidence of spallation between the alloys.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Crack density and spallation frequency measured by SEM
Phase identification and chemical composition via XRD and EDS
Interfacial stress indicators through microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si do not consistently exhibit a thinner, more adherent, and slowly growing oxide layer with fewer cracks and reduced spallation relative to alloys with X = Mn, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Elements (Al, Ta, Nb = 143 p.m. []) with equal atomic radius were added to verify the relationship between solid solution strengthening and atomic size. CoCrFeNiX0.4 (X = Al, Ta, Nb) HEAs with equal entropy were prepared by powder plasma arc additive manufacturing (PPA-AM) and evaluated for their mechanical properties. The following were investigated in order to identify the strengthening mechanism in the developed HEAs: (i) phase crystal structure and texture; (ii) the nanohardness of the FCC and precipitated phase; and (iii) the relationship between eutectic structure, low angle grain boundaries, and deformed grains.
